subject: chemistry
title: Group 7: the halogens
key_idea: The **halogens** are non-metals with seven outer electrons, found as molecules of two atoms. Going down the group the melting and boiling points rise and the reactivity falls. A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive one from its salt solution.

blocks.text: The halogens are fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine and astatine. This section covers their physical properties and the trend down the group.

items.meaning: The elements in Group 7. They have seven electrons in the outer shell, so they have similar reactions.
A negative ion formed when a halogen atom gains one electron, such as Cl⁻.

items: The halogens are non-metals.
They consist of molecules made of pairs of atoms: F₂, Cl₂, Br₂ and I₂.
Going down the group, the relative molecular mass, melting point and boiling point all increase.
The atoms get larger going down the group. Atomic radius: chlorine 0.099 nm, bromine 0.114 nm, iodine 0.133 nm.
Use the pattern to predict astatine: a solid with the formula At₂.

items.text: Going down the group, the molecules get larger.
The intermolecular forces (forces between molecules) increase.
More energy is needed to overcome these forces, so the boiling point is higher.

items: Halogens are non-metals that exist as diatomic molecules.
Melting and boiling points increase down the group.
Fluorine is a gas because it has weak forces between its molecules, which need little energy to overcome.

blocks.text: The halogens react with metals and with non-metals. In each case a halogen atom gains one electron to fill its outer shell.

rows: A metal halide, an ionic compound
A metal halide, an ionic compound
A hydrogen halide, which dissolves in water to form an acidic solution

items: In calcium chloride, each calcium atom loses two electrons to form Ca²⁺.
Each chlorine atom gains one electron to form Cl⁻.
So one calcium atom reacts with two chlorine atoms: CaCl₂.
Both ions have full outer shells.
Halogens react with metals to form metal halides, which are ionic.
Halogens react with hydrogen to form hydrogen halides, such as HCl, which dissolve to give acidic solutions.
A halogen atom gains one electron to form a halide ion with a 1− charge.

blocks.text: Reactivity decreases going down Group 7. This is the opposite of Group 1.

items.text: A halogen higher up the group has fewer shells, so its outer shell is closer to the nucleus.
The nucleus attracts an incoming electron more strongly, with less shielding.
Fluorine gains an electron most easily, so it is the most reactive.

items: A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halogen from a solution of its salt.
Chlorine displaces bromine and iodine. Bromine displaces iodine. Iodine displaces neither.

diagram.alt: Pick a halogen and a salt solution to see whether a displacement reaction happens.
diagram.prompt: Pick a halogen to add to a salt solution

options.label: Chlorine + potassium bromide
results: **Yes**, chlorine is more reactive than bromine

options.label: Chlorine + potassium iodide
results: **Yes**, chlorine is more reactive than iodine

options.label: Bromine + potassium iodide
results: **Yes**, bromine is more reactive than iodine

options.label: Bromine + potassium chloride
results: **No**, bromine is less reactive than chlorine
No change: the solution stays orange

options.label: Iodine + potassium bromide
results: **No**, iodine is less reactive than bromine
No change: the solution stays brown

options.label: Iodine + potassium chloride
results: **No**, iodine is less reactive than chlorine
No change: the solution stays brown

items: Reactivity decreases down Group 7, because the outer shell is further from the nucleus and an electron is gained less easily.
A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halogen from its salt solution.
Chlorine displaces bromine and iodine. Bromine displaces iodine.

checks.q: Give the colour and physical state of bromine at room temperature.
Explain why the boiling points of the halogens increase going down Group 7.
checks.a: The molecules get larger, so the intermolecular forces increase. More energy is needed to overcome them.

checks.q: Write a balanced equation for the reaction between chlorine and sodium iodide solution.

worked_example.question:
A student mixes solutions of halogens with solutions of their salts.

Chlorine with potassium bromide: the solution turns orange.
Chlorine with potassium iodide: the solution turns brown.
Bromine with potassium chloride: no change.
Bromine with potassium iodide: the solution turns brown.
Iodine with potassium chloride: no change.
Iodine with potassium bromide: no change.

Explain how the reactivity of the halogens changes going down Group 7.

Use the results.
answer_points: The reactivity decreases going down Group 7.
Chlorine displaces bromine and iodine (it has two reactions).
Bromine displaces iodine, and iodine does not react (it has no reactions).
worked_example.tip: State the trend, then back it with the results for each halogen.

worked_example.question: Explain why the displacement reactions of halogens are redox reactions.
answer_points: The halide ions lose electrons (are oxidised).
The halogen atoms or molecules gain electrons (are reduced).
worked_example.tip: Half-equations can score either mark. Do not say that the halogen being displaced is reduced.

blocks.text: (Higher tier) In a displacement reaction one substance loses electrons and another gains them. This makes it a redox reaction.

items: Oxidation is loss of electrons. Reduction is gain of electrons.
In Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂, the bromide ions lose electrons, so they are oxidised.
The chlorine gains electrons to form chloride ions, so it is reduced.

blocks.label: Half-equation: bromide ions oxidised
where: Electrons are on the right, so this is oxidation.

blocks.label: Half-equation: chlorine reduced
where: Electrons are on the left, so this is reduction.

worked_example.question:
This question is about elements in Group 7 of the periodic table.

Explain, in terms of the arrangement of electrons, the decrease in reactivity from fluorine to astatine.
answer_points: Fluorine atoms are smaller, so the outer shell is closer to the nucleus (fewer shells, less shielding).
Electrons are more strongly attracted to fluorine atoms, so fluorine gains electrons more easily.
worked_example.tip: Assume an unqualified answer refers to fluorine. Fluorine gaining electrons more quickly is ignored.

worked_example.question:
A student bubbles chlorine gas into a test-tube containing aqueous potassium bromide.
Complete the ionic equation for this reaction. Include state symbols.
______ + ____Br⁻(aq) → ______ + ______
worked_example.tip: One mark for the products Br₂ and Cl⁻, one for balancing and one for the state symbols. The potassium ions do not change, so they are left out of an ionic equation.

items: Going down the group the density increases, as well as the melting and boiling points. Reactivity decreases.
At room temperature chlorine is a pale yellow-green gas, bromine is a red-brown liquid and iodine is a grey-black solid.

blocks.label: Displacement as an ionic equation
where: Chlorine gains electrons and is more reactive than bromine.
Bromide ions lose electrons and become bromine.

worked_example.question:
A student is given an aqueous solution of chlorine and an aqueous solution of potassium bromide.
Explain how he can use these two solutions to compare the reactivity of chlorine with the reactivity of bromine.
answer_points: Add the chlorine solution to the potassium bromide solution
So chlorine is more reactive than bromine
worked_example.tip: Name the product as bromine, not bromide, when you say what is displaced.
